Let \(q_n = 1/\sqrt{a_n}\) where it exists; the sum can be handled directly with \(a_n\) instead.

From the recurrence, \(a_{n+1} = \dfrac{a_n}{(a_n+1)^2}\). Since \(a_n \equiv 396\) would force \(0 \equiv 396\), it never occurs, and \(a_n\) is never 0 because \(a_0=1\) and each step preserves nonzero values. So \(1/a_{n+1} = \dfrac{(a_n+1)^2}{a_n} = a_n + 2 + \dfrac{1}{a_n}\).

Let \(b_n = 1/a_n\). Then \(b_{n+1} = a_n + 2 + b_n\), so

\[ a_n = b_{n+1} - b_n - 2. \]

Summing from \(n=0\) to \(N\) telescopes:

\[ \sum_{n=0}^{N} a_n = b_{N+1} - b_0 - 2(N+1). \]

Here \(b_0 = 1\) and \(N = 2026\). Since \(a_{2026} = 9\), we have \(b_{2026} = 1/9\), and so

\[ b_{2027} = a_{2026} + 2 + b_{2026} = 9 + 2 + \tfrac19 = \tfrac{100}{9}. \]

Modulo 397, \(9 \cdot 44 = 396 \equiv -1\), so \(9^{-1} \equiv -44\). Then

\[ \tfrac{100}{9} \equiv -4400 \equiv -33 \pmod{397}, \]

because \(4400 - 11\cdot 397 = 33\).

The sum is therefore

\[ -33 - 1 - 2\cdot 2027 = -4088 \pmod{397}. \]

Since \(4088 = 10\cdot 397 + 118\), this is \(-118 \equiv 279\).

ANSWER: 279
